correctness.rationale: The kernel calculation (RESULT.md, lines 43–52) gives reciprocal circles centered at s=(1−r²)^−1 of radius R(s); the angle covers every point since m−1 is positive, and the denominator cannot vanish. Recomputing R′ and R″ gives R′²+RR″<α² by the positive tail of the expansion of (1−1/s)^−2(β−1); with D=1−R′²−RR″, the two contact derivatives are D and R′D/sqrt(1−R′²). At height y>0 the right branch covers from s_0=R^−1(y) to infinity in abscissa, while the left branch has derivative with the sign of Y(s)−y. Thus an attained interior minimum gives the entire closed slice, or a decreasing left branch with unattained limit gives the open slice. At y=0 the minimum is s=1. At α=1, R=s−β+β(β−1)/(2s)+O(s^−2) gives the claimed threshold; even at equality the derivative is strictly negative at every finite admissible s. The envelope slope is sqrt(1−R′²)/R′ and strictly decreases. At s=1+t, X−1 is asymptotic to t and Y to αt^β, so inversion gives the stated cusp with its coefficient. At α<1 the expansions give X−(sqrt(1−α²)/α)Y=β+O(s^−1). Inversion gives the limiting angles (at α=1 the limit is vertical) and maps x=β to the claimed diameter circle except for the zero endpoint, which comes only from infinity. All conclusions follow analytically; checker.py was inspected as a finite floating-point diagnostic and not executed.

value.rationale: The canonical monomial family tests the difference between a filled range, its closure and pointwise attainment. Knowing precisely where the left contact radius escapes at unit modulus, and hence which entire arcs (including endpoints) are missing after inversion, answers a question not settled by qualitative cusp or circle filling theorems. The cusp reads off the degree and modulus and the far-field description gives the limiting directions at zero. This is a useful complete range classification, not a resampling of the circles.
